actions.reason: RegexTokenizer.encode_ordinary ran _encode_chunk on each unique chunk, and that rescans the whole chunk for the lowest-index pair before every merge. Suppose every merge creates an id larger than both children and the ids are distinct. Then the lowest-index pair present is always the next merge in index order, the same property BasicTokenizer.encode already relies on. On that path the unique chunks are converted to latin-1 strings, one character per id, and joined with a separator character above every token id, so no merge pair can span two chunks. The merges are applied in index order with str.replace, the result is split back per chunk, and the ids are rebuilt in chunk order. Merge tables that do not meet the ordering condition, and subclasses that override _encode_chunk (GPT4Tokenizer), keep the previous path. Outputs are identical.

diff --git a/minbpe/regex.py b/minbpe/regex.py
--- a/minbpe/regex.py
+++ b/minbpe/regex.py
@@ -293,6 +293,28 @@ class RegexTokenizer(Tokenizer):
         """Encoding that ignores any special tokens."""
         # split text into chunks of text by categories defined in regex pattern
         text_chunks = re.findall(self.compiled_pattern, text)
+        if type(self)._encode_chunk is RegexTokenizer._encode_chunk:
+            # when every merge creates a token id larger than both of its children
+            # (and ids are distinct), the merges can be applied in index order with
+            # str.replace; the unique chunks are joined by a separator character
+            # above every token id, so no pair can span two chunks
+            ordered = sorted(self.merges.items(), key=lambda item: item[1])
+            prev = 255
+            for (p0, p1), idx in ordered:
+                if not (type(p0) is int and type(p1) is int and type(idx) is int
+                        and 0 <= p0 < idx and 0 <= p1 < idx and prev < idx < 0x10ffff):
+                    break
+                prev = idx
+            else:
+                sep = chr(prev + 1)
+                unique = list(dict.fromkeys(text_chunks))
+                s = sep.join([ch.encode("utf-8").decode("latin-1") for ch in unique])
+                for (p0, p1), idx in ordered:
+                    pair = chr(p0) + chr(p1)
+                    if pair in s:
+                        s = s.replace(pair, chr(idx))
+                piece_of = dict(zip(unique, s.split(sep)))
+                return list(map(ord, "".join(map(piece_of.__getitem__, text_chunks))))
         # all chunks of text are encoded separately, then results are joined
         ids = []
         merge_map = build_merge_map(self.merges)

journal.text:
I changed RegexTokenizer.encode_ordinary in minbpe/regex.py, lines 295-297, 3 lines replaced by 25. Before, it ran _encode_chunk on each unique chunk, and that rescans the whole chunk for the lowest-index pair before every merge. The new path assumes every merge creates an id larger than both children and that the ids are distinct. Under that assumption the lowest-index pair present is always the next merge in index order. BasicTokenizer.encode already relies on the same property.

In my sandbox, encode_ir went from 798138487 to 747745859, ratio 0.9369. Outputs were identical. The other metrics moved slightly up: train_basic_ir 1.0020, train_regex_ir 1.0030, decode_ir 1.0023, save_load_ir 1.0031. All were within guard limits. I submitted it and it is waiting on replays.

I now think per-chunk rescanning was the main encode cost.

Next I should check whether the guard path for merge tables that break the id ordering is exercised, and look at encode_ir again after replay.
